values.label: White blood cells (leukocytes), total count
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Characteristics of Leukocytes: “For instance, leukocytes are far less numerous than erythrocytes: Typically there are only 5000 to 10,000 per µ L.”
values.note: µL is a microlitre, a millionth of a litre of blood.

values.label: Neutrophils, share of all white blood cells
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Granular Leukocytes: “The most common of all the leukocytes, neutrophils will normally comprise 50–70 percent of total leukocyte count.”
values.note: This is a share of all white blood cells, not a count. A higher neutrophil count does not by itself mean a higher share, so no condition here gives this row an arrow.

values.label: Lymphocytes, share of all white blood cells
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Agranular Leukocytes: “Lymphocytes are the second most common type of leukocyte, accounting for about 20–30 percent of all leukocytes, and are essential for the immune response.”
values.note: The source says about 20–30 percent. This is a share of all white blood cells, not a count.

states.label: Bacterial infection
states.summary: Neutrophils are rapid responders to infection with a preference for bacteria; abnormally high neutrophil counts indicate infection or inflammation, particularly triggered by bacteria.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Granular Leukocytes: “Neutrophils are rapid responders to the site of infection and are efficient phagocytes with a preference for bacteria.” and “Abnormally high counts of neutrophils indicate infection and/or inflammation, particularly triggered by bacteria, but are also found in burn patients and others experiencing unusual stress.”
states.modelNote: No arrows are shown: the source describes high neutrophil counts, an absolute number of cells, while the rows here give the total of all white cells and each kind’s share of that total, and the source gives no direction for either. The markers show only what the teaching model simulates.

states.label: Viral infection
states.summary: Abnormally high lymphocyte counts are characteristic of viral infections; lymphocytes are essential for the immune response.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Agranular Leukocytes: “Abnormally high lymphocyte counts are characteristic of viral infections as well as some types of cancer.”
states.modelNote: No arrows are shown: the source describes high lymphocyte counts, an absolute number of cells, and gives no direction for the total white cell count or for the lymphocyte share shown here. The markers show only what the teaching model simulates.

states.label: Leukocytosis (raised white blood cell count)
states.summary: Leukocytosis is excessive leukocyte proliferation: more white blood cells are made, so the total white cell count rises.

evidence.wbc: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4, Disorders of Leukocytes: “Excessive leukocyte proliferation is known as leukocytosis”

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Disorders of Leukocytes: “Excessive leukocyte proliferation is known as leukocytosis”
states.modelNote: The model makes more of every kind of white cell, so the total count rises while the shares stay the same. No direction is cited for the two shares, and the model does not move them.

states.label: Leukopenia (too few white blood cells made)
states.summary: In leukopenia too few leukocytes are produced; if it is pronounced, the person may be unable to ward off disease.

evidence.wbc: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4, Disorders of Leukocytes: “Leukopenia is a condition in which too few leukocytes are produced.” and “If this condition is pronounced, the individual may be unable to ward off disease.”

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, Disorders of Leukocytes: “Leukopenia is a condition in which too few leukocytes are produced. If this condition is pronounced, the individual may be unable to ward off disease.”
states.modelNote: The model makes fewer of every kind of white cell, so the shares stay the same. No direction is cited for the two shares, and the model does not move them.
